A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for a month prior to presentation, with a noticeable increase in pallor a week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Systemic examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and a small palpable lymph node in the supraclavicular and inguinal region; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 97 mg/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (platelet 11 × 10⁹/L). White‑blood‑cell count was 10.2 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilic predominance and toxic granulation. Reticulocyte count was elevated at 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑cell fragmentation with schistocytes (1.45 %). Lactate dehydrogenase was markedly elevated at 1,021 U/L; AST 46 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 12.7 µmol/L. Urinalysis showed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was low at 1.72 g/L; Coombs test was negative.

The patient was initially diagnosed with atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and received two doses of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg without response; hemoglobin and platelet counts continued to decline. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed; the aspirate did not suggest malignancy but showed megakaryocytes suggestive of immune destruction. He was started on a six‑day trial of pulse methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day divided twice daily) with no improvement. Bone‑marrow biopsy later revealed peripheral destruction of blood cells consistent with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and a likely diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP); repeat peripheral smear showed schistocytes >2.5 %. A five‑day trial of fresh‑frozen plasma was initiated, resulting in improvement of LDH and platelet levels.

Bone‑marrow biopsy also showed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas, a nonspecific finding that could be due to infections (viral, bacterial, tuberculosis), infiltrative diseases such as sarcoidosis, or malignancy. Viral surveillance for EBV, CMV, and HIV was negative; QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography and contrast‑enhanced chest and abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy. Because Brucella is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, brucella titers were sent.
